initial_assessment: 34-year-old man presenting with approximately one week of headache and vomiting (concerning for raised intracranial pressure) and ECOG performance status 2. MRI (2026-10-17) demonstrates a well-circumscribed, lobulated, extra-axial/cortically based left frontal mass measuring 4.2 x 3.5 x 3.0 cm, plus a discrete 5 mm intensely enhancing nodule on the posterior pial surface of the cervical cord at C6. Stereotactic needle biopsy (2026-10-19) is reported only as 'suggestive of an intracranial mesenchymal tumor with spinal drop metastasis'; the final histologic and molecular entity is explicitly not established on the current material. Both mass-related Conditions are deliberately coded provisional (ICD-10-CM D43.0/D43.4, 'neoplasm of uncertain behavior') and must not be treated as a confirmed diagnosis. Explicit uncertainty: at this time there is no established entity, no WHO grade, no proven stage, and no identified targetable molecular alteration. 'Intracranial mesenchymal tumor' is a descriptive umbrella spanning biologically diverse entities with very different grades, behaviors, and treatments, so no disease-directed therapy can rationally be chosen against an unspecified label. Two findings add urgency: the symptom pattern suggests possible raised intracranial pressure, and the C6 nodule raises the possibility of leptomeningeal (drop) spread, which — if proven — would change stage, treatment intent, and prognosis. Management at this stage is diagnostic confirmation, safe staging, symptom control, and multidisciplinary review, with all disease-directed treatment (chemotherapy or definitive radiotherapy) deferred until entity, grade, extent, and resectability are established.
diagnostic_confirmation_and_staging: 1) Definitive pathology: expedite expert neuropathology review (second opinion/consultation service) of the existing stereotactic cores with complete immunohistochemistry to assess lineage/differentiation, mitotic activity and Ki-67 proliferation index, and necrosis — the results that establish entity and grade. Because limited needle material is a recognized cause of an unclassifiable result, obtain additional tissue if the integrated WHO CNS5 diagnosis cannot be rendered: the superficial, extra-axial left frontal location appears surgically accessible, so an open excisional biopsy/resection (diagnostic and potentially therapeutic) or re-biopsy should be discussed with neurosurgery. 2) Molecular work-up on tumor tissue: DNA methylation profiling (classifier assignment), RNA-based fusion testing (RNA-seq or targeted fusion panel), and targeted DNA sequencing, plus cytogenics where applicable. These are the results that would most directly change management: a disease-defining fusion/translocation, a methylation class assignment, or a characteristic mutation profile would establish the entity and grade, which in turn determine the surgical goal (gross total vs subtotal resection), whether and when adjuvant radiotherapy is indicated, candidacy for targeted or systemic therapy, surveillance intensity, and prognosis. 3) Staging: the craniospinal axis is partially assessed (brain and whole-spine contrast MRI already performed); repeat or confirm imaging as clinically indicated, particularly around any planned procedure. CSF cytology is reasonable only if raised intracranial pressure has been excluded — defer lumbar puncture until neurosurgical review confirms it is safe. If the final entity could represent metastasis from an extracranial soft-tumor/sarcoma primary, targeted systemic staging (chest/abdomen/pelvis CT or PET) should follow once the entity is known. 4) Resectability assessment: formal neurosurgical review of the MRI for dural or venous-sinus involvement, edema, mass effect, midline shift, and relationship to eloquent cortex, with a recommendation for maximal safe resection versus re-biopsy. 5) Baseline studies: CBC, chemistry panel, coagulation studies, medication/allergy review, and pre-anesthetic evaluation if surgery is likely.
immediate_management_plan: Short-horizon plan (days to weeks): diagnostic confirmation, safe staging, symptom control, and multidisciplinary review — explicitly no chemotherapy and no definitive radiotherapy while the entity, grade, extent, and resectability remain unestablished. 1) Symptom control and intracranial pressure management: focused neurologic examination and assessment for raised ICP (including fundoscopic evaluation and review of imaging mass effect); dexamethasone only if there is symptomatic edema or mass effect (with GI prophylaxis), plus antiemetics and analgesia for headache; close monitoring of neurologic status with clear return precautions for deterioration. Anticonvulsant therapy only if a seizure occurs (none documented; no routine prophylaxis). Any signs of impending herniation convert this to a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent decompression regardless of the unspecified diagnosis. 2) Expedite the diagnosis: refer to a multidisciplinary tumor board this week (neuro-oncology, neurosurgery, neuropathology, neuroradiology, radiation oncology); send material for the expert pathology review, immunohistochemistry, and methylation/fusion/sequencing studies outlined above; obtain a neurosurgical opinion on resection versus re-biopsy, favoring a procedure that yields sufficient tissue for an integrated diagnosis. 3) Staging safety: hold CSF sampling until ICP safety is confirmed by neurosurgical review; complete any remaining craniospinal imaging needed for surgical planning. 4) Supportive care: physical/occupational therapy and supportive measures for ECOG PS 2, early involvement of palliative-care/symptom services for comfort and education, and transparent counseling of the patient that the diagnosis is provisional, why additional tissue and molecular testing are needed, and why disease-directed treatment is intentionally deferred rather than omitted. 5) Decision checkpoint: re-image promptly if new or worsening symptoms occur; once the integrated pathology and molecular results, grade, extent (including the status of the C6 nodule), and resectability are known, reconvene the tumor board to define any disease-directed plan. This is an educational tumor-board synthesis of synthetic teaching data, not clinical decision support.
